questions.question: What is the maximum recommended length for a copper UTP Ethernet segment?
questions.explanation: UTP Ethernet is limited to about 100 meters per segment.

correct.explanation: Copper UTP Ethernet is limited to 100 meters per segment per TIA/Ethernet standards.

incorrect.explanation: 10 m is far below the standard UTP limit — 100 m is the exam reference length.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 10 m points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for utp distance.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "utp distance", 100 m satisfies what this question tests — 10 m does not.

incorrect.explanation: 500 m applies to some fiber or legacy specs — not standard copper UTP at 100 m.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Using fiber distance for copper UTP
incorrect.whatItDoes: 500 m points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for utp distance.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "utp distance", 100 m satisfies what this question tests — 500 m does not.

incorrect.explanation: 1 km is fiber territory — copper UTP max is 100 m for exam purposes.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Confusing fiber reach with copper UTP
incorrect.whatItDoes: 1 km points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for utp distance.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "utp distance", 100 m satisfies what this question tests — 1 km does not.

answerReview.examTip: Copper UTP Ethernet segment = 100 m. Know this cold.

questions.question: Which cable type connects a PC to a switch?

correct.explanation: PC (MDI) to switch (MDIX) uses a straight-through cable — like devices need crossover without auto-MDIX.

incorrect.explanation: Crossover is for like-to-like (switch-switch, PC-PC) on legacy gear without auto-MDIX.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Crossover points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for straight-through.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "straight-through", Straight-through satisfies what this question tests — Crossover does not.

incorrect.explanation: Console rollover is for out-of-band management — not LAN data between PC and switch.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Confusing console cable with Ethernet patch
incorrect.whatItDoes: Console rollover points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for straight-through.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "straight-through", Straight-through satisfies what this question tests — Console rollover does not.

incorrect.explanation: Fiber SM is a different media — the question asks typical copper PC-to-switch cabling.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Answering fiber when copper patch is required
incorrect.whatItDoes: Fiber SM only points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for straight-through.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "straight-through", Straight-through satisfies what this question tests — Fiber SM only does not.

answerReview.examTip: PC → switch = straight-through. Like → like (no auto-MDIX) = crossover.

questions.question: Which fiber type is typically used for long-distance WAN links?
questions.explanation: Single-mode fiber (often yellow) supports long laser-based runs.

correct.explanation: Single-mode (yellow jacket) uses a narrow core for long-distance WAN links (km range).

incorrect.explanation: Multimode (orange/aqua) is for shorter campus runs — not long-haul WAN.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Multimode orange points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for sm vs mm.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "sm vs mm", Single-mode yellow satisfies what this question tests — Multimode orange does not.

incorrect.explanation: Cat5 copper is twisted-pair Ethernet — not fiber for long-distance WAN.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Copper Cat5 points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for sm vs mm.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "sm vs mm", Single-mode yellow satisfies what this question tests — Copper Cat5 does not.

incorrect.explanation: Coax is legacy broadband/cable — WAN fiber uses single-mode.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Coax points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for sm vs mm.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "sm vs mm", Single-mode yellow satisfies what this question tests — Coax does not.

answerReview.examTip: Fiber: multimode (orange, short) | single-mode (yellow, long) — match transceiver to cable.

questions.question: Which connector is commonly found on SFP modules?
questions.explanation: LC is the dominant fiber connector on SFP/SFP+ transceivers.

correct.explanation: LC (Lucent Connector) is the dominant SFP/SFP+ fiber connector — small form factor.

incorrect.explanation: RJ-45 is copper Ethernet — SFP modules use fiber connectors like LC.
incorrect.whatItDoes: RJ-45 points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for connector.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "connector", LC satisfies what this question tests — RJ-45 does not.

incorrect.explanation: DB-9 is a serial/console connector — not SFP media.
incorrect.whatItDoes: DB-9 points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for connector.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "connector", LC satisfies what this question tests — DB-9 does not.

incorrect.explanation: USB-C is not used on standard Cisco SFP modules.
incorrect.whatItDoes: USB-C points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for connector.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "connector", LC satisfies what this question tests — USB-C does not.

answerReview.examTip: SFP connectors: LC (most common) | SC (older) — always verify module + cable pairing.

questions.question: Cat6a UTP is associated with which speed at 100 m?
questions.explanation: Cat6a is rated for 10 Gbps at 100 m.

correct.explanation: Cat6a supports 10GBASE-T at 100 m — the exam associates Cat6a with 10 Gbps at standard distance.

incorrect.explanation: 100 Mbps is Cat5e territory — Cat6a targets much higher speeds.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Downgrading Cat6a to Fast Ethernet speed
incorrect.whatItDoes: 100 Mbps gives a numeric value (timer, prefix, or rate) that may not match the fact tested in Cat6a is rated for 10 Gbps at 100 m.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "Cat6a is rated for 10 Gbps at 100 m", 10 Gbps satisfies what this question tests — 100 Mbps does not.

incorrect.explanation: 1 Gbps is common on Cat5e/Cat6 — Cat6a is the 10G copper standard at 100 m.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 1 Gbps points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for Cat6a is rated for 10 Gbps at 100 m.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "Cat6a is rated for 10 Gbps at 100 m", 10 Gbps satisfies what this question tests — 1 Gbps does not.

incorrect.explanation: 40 Gbps over copper UTP at 100 m is not the Cat6a exam pairing — 10 Gbps is.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Jumping to 40G on UTP for Cat6a
incorrect.whatItDoes: 40 Gbps points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for Cat6a is rated for 10 Gbps at 100 m.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "Cat6a is rated for 10 Gbps at 100 m", 10 Gbps satisfies what this question tests — 40 Gbps does not.

questions.question: Two legacy switches without auto-MDIX need which cable?
questions.explanation: Like devices historically required crossover to swap TX/RX pairs.

correct.explanation: Switch-to-switch (like devices) without auto-MDIX requires a crossover cable.

incorrect.explanation: Straight-through connects unlike devices (PC-switch) — two switches need crossover on legacy hardware.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Straight-through points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for crossover.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "crossover", Crossover satisfies what this question tests — Straight-through does not.

incorrect.explanation: Console cable is for management port — not inter-switch Ethernet trunk links.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Using console cable for switch interconnect
incorrect.whatItDoes: Console points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for crossover.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "crossover", Crossover satisfies what this question tests — Console does not.

incorrect.explanation: Serial DCE/DTE is WAN router links — not Ethernet switch-to-switch.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Confusing WAN serial with Ethernet crossover
incorrect.whatItDoes: Serial DCE points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for crossover.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "crossover", Crossover satisfies what this question tests — Serial DCE does not.

answerReview.examTip: Switch ↔ switch (no auto-MDIX) = crossover. Modern gear often auto-MDIX.

questions.question: What is the primary benefit of SFP modules?
choices: Flexible hot-swappable media on a port
questions.explanation: SFPs let you choose copper or fiber media per port without changing the switch.

correct.explanation: SFP modules provide hot-swappable, flexible media — swap fiber/copper without replacing the switch port.

incorrect.explanation: SFP affects port media — it doesn't change CPU speed.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Increase CPU speed points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for sfp purpose.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "sfp purpose", Flexible hot-swappable media on a port satisfies what this question tests — Increase CPU speed does not.

incorrect.explanation: SFP is a physical layer module — it doesn't replace Spanning Tree.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Replace STP points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for sfp purpose.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "sfp purpose", Flexible hot-swappable media on a port satisfies what this question tests — Replace STP does not.

incorrect.explanation: SFP carries Layer 1/2 signals — encryption is a higher-layer function.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Encrypt traffic points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for sfp purpose.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "sfp purpose", Flexible hot-swappable media on a port satisfies what this question tests — Encrypt traffic does not.

answerReview.examTip: SFP/SFP+ = pluggable optics — change distance/speed by swapping the module, not the port.

questions.question: True or False: Multimode fiber is often orange or aqua jacketed.
questions.explanation: True — MM is commonly orange (OM2) or aqua (OM3/OM4); SM is often yellow.

correct.explanation: True — multimode fiber is commonly orange (OM1/OM2) or aqua (OM3/OM4) jacketed.

incorrect.explanation: False is wrong — color coding helps identify multimode vs single-mode (yellow).
incorrect.whatItDoes: False states the opposite of the tested fact about mm color.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "mm color", True satisfies what this question tests — False does not.

answerReview.examTip: Fiber colors: orange/aqua = multimode | yellow = single-mode — verify before connecting.
